passage:
Note left for Chaitanya's parents by their neighbour, Sunday
You asked me to keep an ear out while you were at the wedding. Here is what I saw from my balcony.
At four, the courier rang your bell. Chaitanya spoke through the closed door: "Please leave it with the neighbour, my parents aren't home." He didn't open it.
At five, Irawati from the third floor came up asking him to come to the park. I heard him say, "I have to phone Mummy first. That's the rule." He did, and you said no, so he stayed. He sounded disappointed, but he didn't sneak out.
He didn't touch the stove either, just ate the sandwiches you left. When I checked on him, he said, "I feel so grown up!" I think you can trust him with more.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya tell the courier through the closed door?
qa.a: To leave it with the neighbour because his parents weren't home.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya feel being home alone?
qa.a: Grown up and proud, as he said, though disappointed when he could not go to the park.

qa.q: What did the neighbour suggest to the parents, and why?
qa.a: That they can trust him with more, because he kept every rule while nobody was watching him.

qa.q: How might Irawati have felt when Chaitanya phoned his mother first?
qa.a: Perhaps a bit disappointed, but she saw him keep his parents' rule.

grounding: A neighbour's note shows a boy left home alone who keeps his parents' rules, feels grown up and earns more freedom.

passage:
Thursday
Ammi had to go to the hospital to see Nana, and for the first time she left me home alone for the whole afternoon! Rules: door locked, no stove, homework before TV, phone her at five.
The TV remote was RIGHT THERE. Nobody would know. But Ammi had looked at me as if she was handing me something important. So I did the maths first (twenty sums!), then watched cartoons.
At five I phoned. Ammi's voice went soft when I told her.
When she came home, she saw the finished homework and said, "From next week you can cycle to cricket practice on your own."
I feel ten feet tall, and kind of responsible too. Pallavi next door says I'm showing off. I am, a bit.
Irfan

qa.q: How many sums did Irfan do before watching TV?
qa.a: Twenty sums.

qa.q: How does Irfan feel after being trusted?
qa.a: Proud and grown up, ten feet tall and a bit responsible too.

qa.q: What did keeping the rules earn Irfan?
qa.a: More freedom: cycling to cricket practice alone from next week.

qa.q: How might Ammi have felt when she saw the finished homework?
qa.a: Relieved and proud, ready to trust Irfan with more.

grounding: A child left home alone keeps the parent's rules unobserved, feels grown up and is given more freedom.

passage:
"Homework done?" Mummy called from the kitchen of their Delhi flat.
"Yes!" Jasleen called back, already halfway out of the door to play badminton with Tushar. It wasn't true. Two pages of Hindi were still blank.
The game should have been fun. But every time the shuttle flew up, Jasleen thought of the blank pages. At dinner Mummy said, "Good girl, finishing early," and Jasleen's dal stuck in her throat.
Later she worked it out: tomorrow Ma'am would check, then Ma'am would write a note, then Mummy would see the note. One small lie was turning into three.
At bedtime she went to the kitchen. "Mummy, I lied. I didn't finish the Hindi." Mummy put down the tiffin box. "Thank you for telling me. Sit, I'll stay with you while you do it."
The pages took twenty minutes. Jasleen slept better than she had all evening.

qa.q: What homework was still blank?
qa.a: Two pages of Hindi.

qa.q: What does Jasleen's dal sticking in her throat suggest?
qa.a: She felt guilty and uneasy about the lie, especially when Mummy praised her.

qa.q: How did Jasleen stop the lie from growing?
qa.a: She told Mummy the truth at bedtime and finished the pages with her.

qa.q: How did Mummy respond to Jasleen's confession?
qa.a: She thanked her for telling and stayed with her while she finished.

grounding: A girl uneasy about a small lie sees it growing and fixes it by telling the truth.

passage:
"Shankar, can I tell you something? Promise not to laugh."
"Depends."
"The remote. It wasn't the cat. I dropped it."
"Akka! You told Appa the cat did it! He shouted at poor Pappu!"
"I know." Lakshmi pulled her knees up. "Nobody knows. But I feel all itchy inside."
"So? He'll buy a new remote."
"And every time Pappu comes in, Appa glares at him. Yesterday he didn't even give him milk."
Shankar was quiet. "That's bad."
"It keeps getting bigger. Like a snowball."
"Then tell him. Now, before it gets any bigger."
Lakshmi walked to the verandah. "Appa? The remote... I dropped it. Not Pappu. I'm sorry I lied."
Appa lowered his newspaper and looked at her for a long moment. "Thank you for telling me, kanna. Now go and give Pappu his milk."

qa.q: Whom did Lakshmi blame for the remote?
qa.a: The cat, Pappu.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi mean by feeling "all itchy inside"?
qa.a: She felt guilty and uneasy about the lie even though nobody knew.

qa.q: Why did Shankar say to tell Appa now?
qa.a: Because the lie was growing, with Pappu being punished, and it would only get bigger.

qa.q: How did Appa respond to the truth?
qa.a: He thanked her calmly and told her to give Pappu his milk, putting the unfairness right.

grounding: A girl uneasy about a small lie sees it growing and eases her conscience by telling her father the truth.

passage:
Note to Rajni's mother from the party host, Saturday
I wanted you to know something nice from today's party. While we adults were busy in the kitchen, I stepped out to fetch plates and heard the children in the hall. Salma dared Rajni to sneak into the kitchen and pour salt into the grown-ups' tea. "Don't be a scaredy-cat!" The others chanted, "Rajni! Rajni!"
Rajni went pink. I could see she hated being called a coward. Then she grinned and said, "I'm saving my bravery for the ghost house at the fair. Let's play musical chairs instead." Salma laughed, and the chanting stopped.
Nobody drank salty tea. And Salma still sat next to Rajni for cake. I thought you would like to know.

qa.q: What did Salma dare Rajni to do?
qa.a: Sneak into the kitchen and pour salt into the grown-ups' tea.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel when the children chanted?
qa.a: Embarrassed and afraid of looking like a coward; she went pink.

qa.q: How did Rajni say no without a fight?
qa.a: With a grin and a joke about saving her bravery for the ghost house, and by suggesting musical chairs.

qa.q: How did Salma respond to the refusal?
qa.a: She laughed and still sat next to Rajni for cake, showing the friendship did not depend on the dare.

grounding: A host's note shows a girl dared to do something naughty while adults are away, who fears looking a coward but says no with a joke.

passage:
Saturday
Mummy and Papa went to the market and Thomas came over. He got bored after ten minutes and said, "I dare you to ring every doorbell on our floor and run. Unless you're a chicken."
My stomach went tight. I really didn't want him to think I'm a chicken. But I also imagined old Mrs. Kapoor coming slowly to the door with her walking stick for nothing.
So I flapped my arms and went "BAWK BAWK" and said, "Chicken says no. Chicken says carrom." He laughed so hard he fell off the sofa. Then we played carrom and I won twice.
Funny. He didn't think I was a coward. He thought I was funny.
Nikita

qa.q: What did Thomas dare Nikita to do?
qa.a: Ring every doorbell on their floor and run.

qa.q: Why did Nikita's stomach go tight?
qa.a: Nikita was afraid of Thomas thinking Nikita was a chicken.

qa.q: How did Nikita turn down the dare?
qa.a: With a joke, flapping and clucking and saying, "Chicken says no. Chicken says carrom."

qa.q: How did Thomas react to the joke?
qa.a: He laughed so hard he fell off the sofa and happily played carrom, not thinking Nikita a coward at all.

grounding: A child dared to do something naughty while parents are out fears looking a coward but says no with a joke, and the friend does not mind.

passage:
The community centre in Nikita's village had started an honesty stall run by Urmila Aunty: pencils, erasers and notebooks on a table, prices on a card, and a tin box with a slot. Nobody sat there. "I trust you all," Urmila Aunty had said at the gathering.
Nikita picked up a notebook marked ₹20. She had only fifteen in her pocket. The hall was empty. She could drop in fifteen and nobody would ever know.
Her hand hovered over the slot. The words "I trust you all" felt heavy on her shoulders.
She put the notebook back. That evening she asked her father for five rupees and walked back before the centre closed. She dropped all twenty in and took the notebook, feeling strangely tall.
On the tin someone had stuck a new card: THANK YOU FOR BEING HONEST. Nikita smiled at it.

qa.q: How much did the notebook cost?
How did Nikita feel as her hand hovered over the slot?
qa.a: Tempted, but she felt the heavy weight of being trusted.

qa.q: How did Nikita honour the trust?
qa.a: She put the notebook back, got the missing five rupees and came back to pay the full amount.

qa.q: What does Urmila Aunty's honesty stall show about how she sees the villagers?
qa.a: She trusts them to pay fairly without being watched.

grounding: A girl at a village honesty stall feels the weight of being trusted and honours it by paying the full amount.

passage:
Saturday: On the road above Pema's village, Vinita Aunty's roadside stall had baskets of oranges, a price board and a wooden box. No one minded it. Pema chose six oranges, dropped in her coins and ran to catch her friends.
Sunday: Counting her leftover coins for a pen, Pema froze. Six oranges were thirty rupees. She had put in only twenty. Nobody had seen. Nobody would know. But the box had trusted her, and her face went hot every time she thought of it.
Monday: After school she walked up the road with a ten-rupee note. Vinita Aunty was there, stacking baskets. Pema pushed the note into the box and explained. Vinita Aunty laughed and patted her cheek. "Some weeks the box is short. This week it's exactly right, because of you." She gave Pema one extra orange.

qa.q: How much had Pema put in the box on Saturday?
qa.a: Twenty rupees.

qa.q: Why did Pema's face go hot on Sunday?
qa.a: She felt guilty, knowing the box had trusted her and she had underpaid.

qa.q: How did Pema set things right?
qa.a: She walked back on Monday and paid the missing ten rupees, explaining to Vinita Aunty.

qa.q: How does Vinita Aunty see Pema's return?
qa.a: She is touched and grateful, since the box is sometimes short, so she gives Pema an extra orange.

grounding: A girl who underpays at an unattended village stall feels the weight of being trusted and returns to pay in full.

passage:
Monday: At the busy crossing near school, a traffic policeman in a white uniform blew his whistle and stopped a whole bus with one hand. Elizabeth held her mother's hand a little tighter. He looked so strong, and a bit scary.
Thursday: A police officer, Inspector Rao, visited their class. She showed them her badge and said, "If you are ever lost or in trouble, you can come to us. That's our job." Elizabeth put up her hand. "Even if we're small?" "Especially then."
Saturday: At the Christmas fair, Elizabeth's friend Payal let go of her aunt's hand and vanished into the crowd. Payal's aunt went white. Elizabeth pointed. "There's the police booth!" They ran. Within ten minutes a constable's voice on the loudspeaker had found Payal by the balloon stall.

qa.q: What did the traffic policeman stop with one hand?
qa.a: A whole bus.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel watching the traffic policeman?
qa.a: A mix of respect and slight fear; he seemed strong and a bit scary.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth use what she learned from Inspector Rao?
qa.a: When Payal got lost, she pointed out the police booth so they could get help.

qa.q: How might Payal's aunt have felt when Payal was found?
qa.a: Hugely relieved, after going white with fear.

grounding: A girl who feels respect and slight fear at a police uniform learns that police help children and uses that when a friend gets lost.

passage: Ojas, you went quiet when that policeman walked past? I felt the same at your age. Let your Devika Dadi tell you. When I was small, at the big fair by the river, I let go of my father's hand and was swept away by the crowd. I cried and cried. Then a tall policeman with a lathi and a huge moustache bent down in front of me. I was so frightened of that moustache that I cried louder! But he took off his cap, gave me a sweet from his pocket and said, "Beti, what's your father's name?" He lifted me onto his shoulders and walked through the crowd shouting it, until my father came running. So, Ojas, if you're ever lost, look for the uniform. They are there to help.

qa.q: What did the policeman give young Devika from his pocket?
qa.a: A sweet.

qa.q: How did young Devika feel when the policeman bent down?
qa.a: Frightened, especially of his huge moustache, so she cried louder.

qa.q: What did the policeman do that turned her fear into trust?
qa.a: He took off his cap, gave her a sweet, asked her father's name and carried her on his shoulders to find him.

qa.q: How might Devika's father have felt when he came running?
qa.a: Hugely relieved and grateful to find his daughter safe.

grounding: A grandmother recalls her awe and fear of a policeman as a lost child, and how he helped her find her father.

passage:
Tuesday: At lunch Minakshi whispered, "If you're naughty, the police put you in a jail with rats. My cousin said." Walking home past the police station, Kavitha kept her eyes on her shoes, her heart beating fast.
Wednesday: At dinner she asked Amma, "Do police take away naughty children?" Amma put down her roti. "No, kanna. Police help people. If you're lost, or someone hurts you, they help. Who told you that?" Kavitha explained. Amma laughed gently. "Minakshi's cousin likes stories."
Friday: On the class trip to the police station, Sub-Inspector Mary showed them the wireless set and the helpline number painted on the wall. Minakshi hid behind Kavitha at first, but the officer let them both try on her cap. Walking out, Kavitha waved at the constable at the gate. He waved back.

qa.q: What did Minakshi say police do to naughty children?
qa.a: Put them in a jail with rats.

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel walking past the police station on Tuesday?
qa.a: Nervous; she kept her eyes on her shoes and her heart beat fast.

qa.q: What helped Kavitha replace the scary story with facts?
qa.a: Asking Amma at dinner, and then visiting the police station on the class trip.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt on the trip?
qa.a: Scared at first, hiding behind Kavitha, then more at ease after trying on the cap.

grounding: A girl made nervous by friends' scary stories about police asks her parent and learns that a good officer helps children.

passage: Devika, your friends say the police will catch you for picking the neighbour's jamun? Ha! Let your Neelam Nani tell you. When I was your age, my cousins told me the thanedar kept naughty children in a cage behind the police chowki. Every time I saw a khaki uniform on the village road, I ran and hid in the sugarcane. Then one monsoon our buffalo was stolen. Bapu went to the chowki, and I went with him, shaking. The thanedar gave me a glass of water and listened to Bapu, and three days later he rode into our courtyard leading our buffalo by the rope. I asked him, "Where is the cage?" He laughed till his cap fell off. "There is no cage for children, beti. We are here to help you." So, Devika, ask your Amma what police really do.

qa.q: What did the thanedar bring back three days later?
qa.a: Their stolen buffalo.

qa.q: How did young Neelam feel whenever she saw a khaki uniform?
qa.a: Scared, so she ran and hid in the sugarcane.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Nani's story?
qa.a: Going with Bapu to the chowki and seeing the thanedar help get their buffalo back.

qa.q: How did the thanedar react to the question about the cage?
qa.a: He laughed till his cap fell off and explained that police are there to help children.

grounding: A grandmother recalls how scary stories made her fear the police until she saw an officer help her family.

passage:
Monday
Traffic week at school! Today we learnt what the lights mean and how to cross at the zebra crossing, looking right, left, right again. We even did a pretend crossing in the playground.
After school Karthik Mama picked me up on his scooter. At the big signal it turned red, and he started to go because the road looked empty. I said, "Mama, red means stop, even if nobody's there!" in my most polite voice.
He braked and laughed. "Okay, traffic inspector." But he waited.
Then a cycle came whooshing round the corner, right where we would have been. Mama went quiet. At home he told Mummy, "Your child saved me today."
I feel proud. And a bit scared about the cycle.
Lokesh

qa.q: What did Lokesh say to Mama at the red light?
qa.a: "Mama, red means stop, even if nobody's there!"

qa.q: How does Lokesh feel after the ride?
qa.a: Proud, and a bit scared about the cycle that came round the corner.

qa.q: How did Lokesh remind Mama about the rule?
qa.a: Politely, simply saying that red means stop.

qa.q: How did Karthik Mama's view change after the cycle whooshed past?
qa.a: He went from joking about a traffic inspector to seeing that the rule had kept them safe.

grounding: A child learns to respect traffic lights and politely reminds an adult who is about to break the rule.

passage:
In the market town of Sagar, the new zebra crossing outside the bus stand had only been painted last month, and most people ignored it. Ankita's Dada, Jagdish, was one of them. He always marched straight across wherever he liked, waving at trucks to slow down.
Today Ankita tugged his kurta. "Dada, the crossing is right there. Madam said at school we should cross only there, and look right, left and right again."
Dada grumbled. "In my day there were no stripes."
"There were fewer trucks too," Ankita said politely.
Dada stared at her, then laughed and let her lead him twenty steps to the stripes. They waited while a bus roared past. On the other side a shopkeeper clapped. "Taught your Dada something, bitiya?"

qa.q: When was the zebra crossing painted?
qa.a: Only last month.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel as she tugged Dada's kurta?
qa.a: Worried about his safety but respectful, so she spoke politely.

qa.q: How did Ankita remind Dada of the rule without being rude?
qa.a: She explained what they had learnt at school and answered his grumble gently.

qa.q: How did Dada react to being reminded?
qa.a: He grumbled at first, then laughed and let her lead him to the crossing.

grounding: A girl who has learnt to cross at zebra crossings politely reminds her grandfather to follow the rule.

passage:
Monday: At the ration office, Karthik and Appa waited in line for two hours. When they reached the window, the clerk didn't look up. "Wrong form. Come next week." When Appa politely asked which form, the clerk snapped, "Can't you read?" and waved them away. Karthik's hands balled into fists. He wanted to shout that Appa reads Tamil and English. But the clerk had the stamp, and they had nothing.
Tuesday: Karthik told his friend Pankaj. "He was rude just because he could be," Karthik said, still hot. Pankaj nodded. "My mother says a stamp doesn't make someone right."
The next Monday: Appa went back with the correct form and a written complaint for the senior officer. Karthik watched him stay calm. The senior officer apologised and stamped the card in five minutes.

qa.q: How long did Karthik and Appa wait in line?
qa.a: Two hours.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel when the clerk snapped at Appa?
qa.a: Angry and powerless; his hands balled into fists, but the clerk had the stamp.

qa.q: How did Appa handle the unfairness safely?
qa.a: He stayed calm, came back with the correct form and gave a written complaint to the senior officer.

qa.q: What did Pankaj's mother's saying mean?
qa.a: That having power, like a stamp, does not make someone right.

grounding: A boy angry and powerless at an official's rudeness to his father sees his father handle it calmly and properly.

passage: Gopika, you're still angry at the guard who shouted at your Amma at the hospital gate? Come, your Charu Ammamma understands. When I was your age, the land clerk came to our village to measure fields. He called my father an "illiterate fool" in front of everyone, because Appa asked him to measure again. My face burned. I wanted to throw a stone at his big umbrella. I felt so small and helpless. But Appa only folded his hands and said, "Sir, I will come to the taluk office." The next week he went with the village elders and a written paper. The officer there made the clerk measure again, and Appa got his correct land. A big post doesn't make someone right, Gopika. And your Amma will handle that guard the proper way, with the hospital manager.

qa.q: What did the land clerk call young Charu's father?
qa.a: An "illiterate fool".

qa.q: How did young Charu feel when the clerk insulted her father?
qa.a: Angry, small and helpless; her face burned and she wanted to throw a stone.

qa.q: What choice in Ammamma's story fixed the unfairness?
qa.a: Appa stayed calm and went to the taluk office with the village elders and a written paper.

qa.q: How might Appa have felt when he was insulted?
qa.a: Hurt and humiliated, but he chose to stay calm and use the proper way.

grounding: A grandmother recalls feeling angry and powerless when an official insulted her father, and how he handled it safely through proper channels.

passage:
"Good morning, children!"
"Good morning, Shivraj Bhaiya!" Chaitanya waved.
Hrithik kept walking. "You know the guard's name?"
"Of course. He's been here since we moved in. He greets everyone, every single day."
"So? It's his job."
"Is it his job to remember my birthday? He saluted me on my birthday."
Hrithik snorted. "Okay, that's nice."
"And when I forgot my key last month, he let me sit in his cabin and gave me his biscuit till Mummy came."
Hrithik looked back at the gate. Shivraj Bhaiya was helping an old man with his bags.
"Where's his village?"
"Ask him yourself."
That afternoon, coming back from school, Hrithik stopped at the gate. "Good afternoon, Shivraj Bhaiya. Where's your village?"
Shivraj Bhaiya's face lit up. "Near Almora, beta! Mountains everywhere."

qa.q: What did Shivraj Bhaiya do when Chaitanya forgot the key?
qa.a: Let Chaitanya sit in his cabin and shared his biscuit until Mummy came.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik look back at the gate?
qa.a: He was curious and surprised, starting to see the guard as a real person.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya show respect in a way Hrithik could learn from?
qa.a: By greeting Shivraj Bhaiya by name every day and remembering his kindness.

qa.q: How might Shivraj Bhaiya have felt when Hrithik asked about his village?
qa.a: Delighted and respected; his face lit up.

grounding: A child greets the building guard by name every day, showing respect for him whatever his job, and a friend learns to do the same.

passage:
I'm Raghav. For a whole year I walked past the man at our building gate without really seeing him. He said "Good morning" every day; I nodded, sometimes.
Then one rainy evening my friend Kunal and I were stuck at the gate, soaked, because the lift was broken. The guard pulled out two dry plastic chairs and made us sit in his little shed. He told us about his daughter, who is in Class 3 back in his village and wants to be a pilot. His name was Anand. I'd never even asked.
Now I say, "Good morning, Anand Uncle," every day. He grins every time and asks about my cricket. It feels strange that for a whole year I didn't know his name. Respect, I think, starts with a name.

qa.q: What does Anand Uncle's daughter want to be?
qa.a: A pilot.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel realising the guard's name had never been asked?
qa.a: Strange and a little ashamed about walking past him for a whole year.

qa.q: What changed in how Raghav treats Anand Uncle?
qa.a: Raghav now greets him by name every day and chats with him.

qa.q: How does Anand Uncle respond to being greeted by name?
qa.a: He grins every time and asks about Raghav's cricket.

grounding: A child who ignored the building guard learns his name and greets him daily, learning to respect everyone whatever their job.

passage:
Monday: The school-van uncle dropped Rajni and Dilnaz at the corner, far from the school gate, so he could go for tea. "Don't tell your parents," he said. "It's our secret. Children must obey elders." Rajni nodded, but her stomach stayed knotted all day.
Wednesday: He stopped near the school lane and told Rajni to stay alone in the van while he went into a shop. "And not a word to anyone." Rajni's heart hammered. Obey, said one voice. This feels wrong, said another. She grabbed her bag, said "No," climbed out with Dilnaz and walked straight to the school gate. She told the class teacher everything. The teacher thanked her, phoned both mothers at once, and the principal stopped that van before home time.
Friday: A new van driver waved them in. Mummy squeezed Rajni's hand. "You chose safety. That was exactly right."

qa.q: Where did the van uncle drop Rajni and Dilnaz on Monday?
qa.a: At the corner, far from the school gate.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling when told to stay alone in the van?
qa.a: Torn and frightened; one voice said obey, another said it felt wrong, and her heart hammered.

qa.q: What did Rajni do, and what did the adults do the same day?
qa.a: She said no, left the van with Dilnaz and told the class teacher, who phoned both mothers; the principal stopped the van before home time.

qa.q: How did Mummy see Rajni's choice?
qa.a: As exactly right, because Rajni chose safety over obeying the driver.

grounding: A girl told by an adult to keep a secret and do something that feels wrong is torn, but says no, leaves and tells a trusted adult.

passage: Shreya, you asked if you must always obey grown-ups? Let your Hemant Chacha tell you something. When I was a boy, a landlord's man stopped me on the canal road. He gave me a tied cloth bundle and said, "Take this to the shed behind the mill. Tell nobody, not even your mother. Good boys obey elders." My legs went shaky. We were taught never to argue with elders, but my stomach said something was wrong. So I put the bundle down on the road, said "No," and ran all the way home. I told my mother. She didn't scold. That same evening she took me to the sarpanch, who called the police. So, Shreya: if a grown-up wants a secret that feels wrong, say no, walk away and tell us.

qa.q: Where was young Hemant told to take the bundle?
qa.a: To the shed behind the mill.

qa.q: What did young Hemant feel when the man gave him the bundle?
qa.a: Torn and scared; his legs went shaky because he was taught to obey elders but felt something was wrong.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Chacha's story?
qa.a: Putting the bundle down, saying no, running home and telling his mother.

qa.q: How did Hemant's mother respond when he told her?
qa.a: She did not scold; she took him to the sarpanch that same evening, and the sarpanch called the police.

grounding: An uncle recalls being told by an adult to keep a secret that felt wrong, and how saying no and telling his mother kept him safe.
